title: Two Sum
description: Find two numbers adding to target
keyInsight: Use a hash map to look up the complement (target - num) in O(1) time while iterating in a single pass.
commonPitfalls: Using the same element twice (e.g. target=6, num=3)
Assuming the array is sorted
Returning values instead of 0-based indices
hints: Can you check if the complement (target - current_num) has already been seen in O(1) time?
Store each number's index in a hash map as you iterate.
If target - num is in map, return [map[target - num], current_index].

title: Contains Duplicate
description: Check if any value appears twice
keyInsight: Store seen elements in a hash set; if an element is already in the set, a duplicate is found immediately.
commonPitfalls: Using nested O(n^2) loops
Sorting first (which takes O(n log n)) when O(n) space is acceptable
hints: What data structure provides O(1) average lookup and insert?
Add each number to a set as you iterate.
If the number is already in the set, return true immediately.

title: Valid Anagram
description: Check if t is anagram of s
keyInsight: Count frequency of each character using a fixed-size 26-int array or hash map; verify all counts match zero.
commonPitfalls: Strings with unequal lengths (return false immediately)
Unicode/special characters if using fixed 26-element array
hints: If lengths differ, can they be anagrams?
Count character frequencies in s, and decrement frequencies with t.
Check if all frequency counts equal zero.

references.title: Valid Anagram - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Group Anagrams
description: Group anagram strings together
timeComplexity: O(n * k log k) or O(n * k)
keyInsight: Use either sorted string or character count tuple '#1#0#2...' as canonical hash key to group words.
commonPitfalls: Mutating original strings
Inefficient key formatting causing hash collisions
Empty string edge cases
hints: What canonical representation is identical for all anagrams?
You can sort each string as a key, or use a 26-count tuple as key in a hash map.
Collect all strings sharing the same key into a list.

references.title: Group Anagrams - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Find k most frequent elements
keyInsight: Count frequencies with a map, then use Bucket Sort where bucket index is frequency (0 to n) to achieve O(n) instead of O(n log k) heap.
commonPitfalls: Using O(n log n) sorting
Index out of bounds if bucket array isn't sized n + 1
hints: Can a frequency ever exceed the length of the array n?
Create an array of buckets of size n + 1, where index i holds elements that appear i times.
Iterate buckets from right (highest frequency) to collect k elements.

references.title: Top K Frequent Elements - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Product of array except self without division
keyInsight: Calculate running prefix products in the output array, then multiply in-place by running suffix products from the right.
commonPitfalls: Using the division operator (forbidden by problem constraint)
Handling zeroes properly if attempting division
hints: The product at i is (product of elements before i) * (product of elements after i).
First pass: populate output[i] with prefix product of elements left of i.
Second pass: maintain a running suffix product from right to left and multiply.

references.title: Product of Array Except Self - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Valid Sudoku

keyInsight: Use bitmasks or sets for rows, cols, and 3x3 sub-boxes indexed by (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3).
commonPitfalls: Off-by-one indexing into 3x3 sub-boxes
Checking unfilled '.' cells instead of skipping them
hints: Only validate pre-filled numbers; ignore empty '.' cells.
How to identify which 3x3 sub-grid cell (r, c) belongs to? Try (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3) or (r // 3, c // 3).
Use 9 sets for rows, 9 for cols, and 9 for boxes to check duplicates.

title: Encode and Decode Strings

Parsing numbers with multi-digit lengths

When decoding, read until '#', parse the length integer N, and take the next N characters.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Length of longest consecutive elements sequence in O(n)
keyInsight: Convert nums to a hash set. Only attempt to build sequences starting at numbers that have no left neighbor (num - 1 not in set).
commonPitfalls: Checking every number without the (num - 1 not in set) condition, leading to O(n^2) worst case on consecutive ranges
hints: Put all numbers in a HashSet for O(1) membership lookup.
How do you know if a number is the START of a sequence?
Only count sequence length starting from x if (x - 1) is NOT in the set.

input.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

commonPitfalls: Creating an auxiliary string (uses O(n) space)
Case sensitivity gotchas (e.g. '0P' is not palindrome)
hints: Can you do this in O(1) space with two pointers?
Move left pointer rightward and right pointer leftward while characters are non-alphanumeric.
Compare character lowercases; if mismatch, return false.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description: Find two numbers in sorted array adding to target
keyInsight: Since array is sorted, sum = nums[l] + nums[r]. If sum > target, r--; if sum < target, l++.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting problem uses 1-indexed output
Using binary search when two pointers is cleaner O(n)
hints: Because the array is already sorted, how does moving l or r affect the sum?
If nums[l] + nums[r] > target, moving r left decreases the sum.
If sum < target, moving l right increases the sum.

title: 3Sum
description: Find all unique triplets summing to 0
keyInsight: Sort the array. Fix the first element nums[i] and use two pointers for remaining two. Skip duplicates for i, l, and r.
commonPitfalls: Generating duplicate triplets
Not skipping duplicate values of nums[i], nums[l], or nums[r]
Missing edge case where nums[i] > 0
hints: Sort the array first to enable two pointers and duplicate skipping.
For each i from 0 to n-3, if nums[i] > 0, break.
Run two-pointer search on subarray [i+1, n-1] for target -nums[i], skipping duplicates whenever a valid triplet is added.

references.title: 3Sum - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Container With Most Water
description: Max water container
keyInsight: Area is constrained by min(h[l], h[r]). Moving the taller pointer can never increase area; always move the shorter pointer inwards.
commonPitfalls: Moving both pointers at once
Trying brute-force O(n^2)
hints: Start with maximum width: l = 0, r = n - 1.
The water height is limited by min(height[l], height[r]).
To find a potentially larger area with smaller width, you MUST find a taller boundary — so move the shorter line inward.

references.title: Container With Most Water - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Compute water trapped after raining
keyInsight: Maintain leftMax and rightMax with two pointers. Process the side with the smaller max bound, adding max - current.
commonPitfalls: Using auxiliary prefix/suffix max arrays (which is O(n) space instead of O(1))
Off-by-one errors on boundaries
hints: Water trapped above index i is max(0, min(max_left, max_right) - height[i]).
Can you maintain max_left and max_right dynamically with two pointers?
If leftMax < rightMax, we know leftMax is the bottleneck for index l, so add leftMax - height[l] and increment l.

references.title: Trapping Rain Water - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description: Max profit from buying and selling one share
keyInsight: Track min_price seen so far; at each day, profit = price - min_price; update max_profit.
commonPitfalls: Selling before buying
Brute-force O(n^2) nested loop
hints: Track the minimum price seen so far as you iterate through the days.
At day i, what is the maximum profit if you sold today?
Update max_profit = max(max_profit, price[i] - min_price).

references.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Length of longest substring without repeating chars
keyInsight: Sliding window with map storing last seen index of characters. When duplicate seen at r, jump l to max(l, lastSeen[c] + 1).
commonPitfalls: Moving l backward if lastSeen[c] is before current l (must use max(l, lastSeen + 1))
Empty string input
hints: Use a sliding window [l, r] and a map of {char: last_seen_index}.
When character at r was already seen at index j >= l, shrink window by jumping l = j + 1.
Update max_len = max(max_len, r - l + 1).

references.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: Longest substring after k replacements
keyInsight: Window is valid if (window_len - max_frequency_char) <= k. Maintain max_freq without needing to decrement on shrink.
commonPitfalls: Recalculating max frequency on every shrink (not needed because window size only matters when max_freq grows)
hints: How many characters do you need to replace in window [l, r]? Exactly (r - l + 1) - max_frequency.
If (r - l + 1) - max_freq > k, the window is invalid: decrement count[s[l]] and advance l.
The maximum window size seen is your answer.

references.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Permutation in String
description: Check if s2 contains a permutation of s1
keyInsight: Fixed-size sliding window of length len(s1). Track matching character counts using a 26-array and a 'matches' counter.
commonPitfalls: Comparing entire frequency maps in O(26) on every step instead of tracking matches variable in O(1)
hints: Window size in s2 must be exactly len(s1).
Count char frequencies of s1 and initial window of s2.
Slide window one char right: add new char count, subtract outgoing char count, and check if matches == 26.

references.title: Permutation in String - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Minimum window in s containing all chars of t
keyInsight: Expand r until window contains all required chars (have == need). Then shrink l while valid to find minimal length.
commonPitfalls: Not checking character frequencies (t can contain duplicates like 'AA')
Off-by-one on slicing substring
hints: Track target character frequencies in a map `need` and current window in `have_map`.
Maintain a counter `have` representing how many unique chars currently satisfy their required frequency.
When have == need.size, record candidate window and shrink from left while maintaining validity.

references.title: Minimum Window Substring - Classic Algorithm Design

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Max value in each sliding window of size k
keyInsight: Use a Monotonic Decreasing Deque storing indices. Elements smaller than current are popped from back; out-of-window popped from front.
commonPitfalls: Storing values instead of indices in deque (indices are needed to check if front is out of window [i - k + 1, i])
hints: Maintain a deque of indices where values are strictly decreasing.
Before adding index i: remove indices from front if they fell out of window (idx < i - k + 1).
Remove indices from back while nums[back] < nums[i], then push i. Deque front is always window max.
